title: When You’re Not Sure
summary: Trade doubt for wonder when you don’t have the answer yet.
script:
Hi. Good to have you back here.
Find a position that feels good for you. Let your body become still and begin to relax.
Close your eyes, or let your gaze rest softly, unfocused.
Nothing to prepare for. Nothing to solve. Just a few quiet minutes, for you.
Inhale slowly.
And exhale, letting your shoulders soften as you do.
One more time. Inhale… and exhale.
I want you to think, for a moment, about the last time you weren't sure about something. Maybe a decision you had to make. Maybe something is sad, and weren't sure how it landed. Maybe just a quiet uncertainty about how your day, or your week, was going to go.
Bring that moment gently into your mind.
Now think about how you talked to yourself about it.
For many people, not knowing can quickly become uncomfortable. You might think, “Why can't I be sure?” or “Why don't I know what to do?” When you start questioning yourself like this, you may begin to doubt.
To doubt means to feel unsure about something or to question whether something is true or right. For example, you might think, “Did I make the right decision?” or “Can I really do this?” That is doubt.
Notice if that heavy kind of questioning feels familiar. No need to judge it. Just notice it.
Inhale slowly.
Now, I want to offer you a different way of holding uncertainty, one that feels lighter.
Imagine a child, maybe five or six years old, looking up at the night sky for the first time. They don't know what stars are made of. They don't understand distance, or space, or anything scientific about it at all.
But notice, they're not distressed by not knowing it. They're not doubting themselves for not having the answer. They're just looking up, quietly amazed, thinking, "I wonder what that is."
That open, curious kind of not-knowing, that is called wonder. To wonder means you hold a question gently, with curiosity instead of pressure, like looking up at something vast and beautiful, comfortable with not having every answer right away.
Exhale slowly.
Notice the difference between the two. Doubt feels tight, and urgent, like something is wrong, and needs fixing immediately. Wonder feels open, and spacious, like there's plenty of time to simply look, and notice, without needing to solve anything right now.
Inhale again.
Let's go back to that moment you thought about earlier. Maybe it was a decision you had to make, something you said, or something you were, you're still not sure about.
Instead of asking yourself, “Why don't I know this already?”, try asking, “I wonder how this will turn out. I wonder how this will turn out.”
You can do the same thing with your English.
Instead of thinking, “Why don't I know these English words?”, try thinking, “I wonder how many new words I'll learn by the end of this practice.”
Notice how different that feels.
The situation is the same. You still don't know the answer. But instead of putting pressure on yourself, you're becoming curious about what might happen.
Exhale slowly.
This is a kind of kindness you can practice, talking to your own uncertainty with wonder, instead of doubt. Not forcing yourself to have answers you don't have yet. Just allowing yourself not to know, calmly, the way that a child looks up at the stars, curious, completely at peace with the mystery of it.
Inhale slowly.
Think of something else right now, in your own life, that still feels unclear. Maybe about your future, maybe about a relationship, maybe simply about yourself.
Instead of demanding an answer immediately, just let yourself wonder about it, gently. "I wonder what will happen." "I wonder what I'll learn from this."
Notice how much lighter this uncertainty feels, held this way.
Exhale completely.
You don't have to eliminate doubt completely, it will probably still visit sometimes, that's alright, it's a very human thing. But you can practice reaching for wonder instead, more and more, whenever uncertainty shows up, the same gentle curiosity you'd offer a child looking up at something vast, and unknown, and quietly beautiful.
And here are a few beautiful words for you to repeat:
I don't need every answer right now.
I just wonder what I'll learn from this.
Not knowing doesn't mean something is wrong with me.
I can hold uncertainty gently, like looking up at the stars.
Take one more slow inhale.
And exhale, completely.
Before we finish, think of one question you don't have the answer to yet. You don't need to answer it now.
Just say quietly to yourself, “I wonder…” And leave the question there.
Take one last slow breath in.
And breathe out.
When you're ready, open your eyes.
As you continue your day, remember: you don't always need to know what comes next.
Sometimes, you can simply wonder.
Maybe the answer will come tomorrow. Maybe next week. Maybe you'll discover something you didn't expect.
For now, it's okay not to know.
Stay curious.

vocabulary.definition: to feel unsure about something or to question whether something is true or right
to hold a question gently, with curiosity instead of pressure
